strengths: BrepCoder addresses a practically relevant problem: directly reasoning over industry-standard B-rep geometry with one language-model-based framework rather than maintaining separate architectures for each CAD task.

The combination of UV-Net features, CoCa-style code/geometry alignment, a Qwen2.5 backbone, and Python-like CAD programs is technically coherent. Representing design histories as code is well motivated and allows the method to exploit pretrained code-generation capabilities.

The reverse-engineering results are promising. Against the most relevant B-rep baseline, CADCL, BrepCoder improves median Chamfer distance from 0.972 to 0.499 and parameter accuracy from 81.52 to 81.93, while producing geometrically plausible sequences despite CAD-history ambiguity.

The paper evaluates four tasks and includes useful ablations of alignment objective, encoder freezing, model scale, projector depth, and Stage-1 initialization. The CAD-history ambiguity examples also correctly expose limitations of exact command-sequence metrics.
The manuscript is generally clear, well organized, visually legible, and appropriately relates the approach to recent CAD reconstruction and CAD-oriented language models.
weaknesses: The downstream comparisons are not sufficiently controlled. For completion, BrepCoder receives the complete target B-rep while CAD-Llama receives only a textual description and code prefix; for error correction, BrepCoder receives exact B-rep geometry whereas GPT/Gemini receive a single rendering, and ReCAD uses a different syntax and dataset. The large gains therefore conflate the proposed training strategy with substantially richer input information.

The evidence for the claimed benefit of the two-stage strategy is weak. Removing Stage 1 changes completion accuracy only from 92.96/87.94 to 92.53/87.91, and produces mixed error-correction results, including better command accuracy and invalid ratio without Stage 1. Only CAD-QA shows a large improvement. Multiple seeds or uncertainty estimates are absent, so several small differences may not be meaningful.

The claimed generalization and general-purpose-agent scope is overstated. Most generative experiments use one DeepCAD-derived distribution and synthetically constructed masks or errors; there is no cross-dataset, out-of-distribution, real-world B-rep, or unseen-operation evaluation. It is also unclear whether Stage 2 is one jointly trained multi-task model or separate task-specific fine-tunes, which is central to the claimed unified framework.

Reproducibility details are substantially incomplete: optimizer, learning rates, schedules, batch sizes, epoch counts, fine-tuning method and frozen components, task-mixture ratios, prompts, decoding settings, parameter tolerance delta, corruption distributions, and compute are not reported. Dataset/code release information is also absent.

Metric reporting is ambiguous. Invalid Ratio values mix entries such as 12.08, 13.98, 0.009, and 0.007 without specifying whether they are percentages or fractions, making the claimed orders-of-magnitude improvement difficult to interpret. Statistical variance is not reported, and the CAD-QA test set appears to contain only about 100 models, making percentage comparisons unstable.

CAD-QA reaches 79%, below PointLLM's 81%; without confidence intervals, category-level analysis, or stronger B-rep-specific baselines, the result does not establish superior reasoning. Likewise, reverse engineering improves geometric distance but not command accuracy over CADCL.

Methodological originality is moderate rather than high: most components—UV-Net, CoCa alignment, a standard MLP projector, Qwen, and the Python-like representation—are adopted from prior work. The main novelty is their integration and multi-task application, but the current evaluation does not yet isolate that integration convincingly enough for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant computer-vision/CAD problem: directly reasoning over industry-standard B-reps rather than relying only on rendered images or point clouds. The unified interface spanning reverse engineering, completion, correction, and question answering is appealing. On DeepCAD, BrepCoder reports strong geometric reconstruction results, including median Chamfer distance of 0.499 versus 0.972 for CADCL, improved parameter accuracy, and a substantially lower reported invalid ratio.

Encoding modeling histories as Python-like code is sensible and may exploit useful priors in a pretrained code-capable LLM. The modeling-ambiguity examples also correctly illustrate why exact command matching can undervalue geometrically equivalent outputs.

The paper is generally understandable and includes ablations for alignment strategy, encoder freezing, LLM size, projector depth, and Stage-1 pretraining. Achieving competitive CAD-QA accuracy with a 1.5B backbone is encouraging.
weaknesses: Under the default Algorithms/General category, the technical novelty is limited. The method mainly assembles UV-Net, CoCa-style alignment, an MLP projector, Qwen2.5, and the previously proposed CAD-Llama code representation. The two-stage alignment/fine-tuning recipe is also conventional, so the submission needs particularly rigorous evidence to establish a substantive contribution.

Several principal comparisons are not controlled. For completion, BrepCoder receives the target B-rep, whereas CAD-Llama receives a textual description; for error correction, BrepCoder receives the complete B-rep while GPT/Gemini receive one rendered view, and ReCAD is evaluated on a different dataset and programming language. These results primarily demonstrate that privileged 3D geometry is more informative than text or one image, not that the proposed architecture or training method is superior.

The Stage-1 ablation weakens the central claim that reverse-engineering pretraining broadly benefits downstream tasks. Completion changes only from 92.53/87.91 to 92.96/87.94, while error-correction command accuracy and invalid ratio become worse. Only CAD-QA improves clearly. Moreover, completion accuracy is inconsistent between Table 2 (92.69) and Table 3 (92.96).

The invalid-ratio reporting appears inconsistent or at least seriously underspecified: prior methods have values such as 12.08 and 13.98, while BrepCoder is reported as 0.009, with no indication that baseline percentages and the proposed method's fractions were normalized to common units. The magnitude of the claimed validity improvement therefore cannot be trusted without clarification.

The claimed generalization and general-purpose CAD-agent capability is not demonstrated. Generation tasks use the synthetic DeepCAD distribution, completion and correction supply B-reps derived from the desired final object, and there is no evaluation on real industrial B-reps, distribution shifts, unseen operation families, noisy geometry, or substantially more complex CAD histories.

Experimental details are inadequate for reproduction: optimization schedules, learning rates, epochs, batch sizes, hardware, tokenizer/context handling, prompt templates, temperature, parameter tolerance, corruption distributions, decoding settings, baseline prompting, and run-to-run variation are absent. No confidence intervals or repeated runs are reported; the CAD-QA test split may contain only about 100 models.

The architecture description contains important ambiguities. For example, concatenating an N-by-128 node tensor with a 1-by-128 global tensor requires an unstated broadcasting operation, and the captioning decoder is described as using the final EOS representation as its query while simultaneously performing autoregressive generation. The training and inference paths need a precise account.

There are no ablations isolating whether gains arise from CoCa alignment, the pretrained LLM, access to the full B-rep, or simply additional training and capacity against matched alternatives. A B-rep-conditioned CAD-Llama or UV-Net-plus-standard-decoder baseline would be especially important.

Overall, the idea has merit, but unfair comparisons, weak support for the central two-stage claim, metric inconsistencies, limited novelty, and insufficient reproducibility leave the scientific case materially incomplete. These are consequential issues rather than presentation-only corrections.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/5c45a3b6ed9c4676a014ecc8458b647f/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses an important and practically relevant vision/CAD problem: reasoning directly from industry-standard B-rep geometry within one language-model framework.

BrepCoder supports an unusually broad set of tasks—reverse engineering, completion, error correction, and CAD question answering—without introducing separate task-specific architectures. The Python-like representation is also a sensible way to exploit pretrained code knowledge.

Reverse-engineering results are promising: the reported median Chamfer distance improves from CADCL's 0.972 to 0.499, parameter accuracy reaches 81.93%, and generated programs are generally executable. The discussion and examples of sequence ambiguity appropriately explain why command accuracy alone can undervalue geometrically equivalent predictions.

The downstream results are strong, particularly for completion (92.69 command and 87.94 parameter accuracy) and synthetic error correction (99.08 and 93.74, respectively). Achieving 79% CAD-QA accuracy with a 1.5B model is competitive with substantially larger point-cloud models.

The paper is clearly organized, its architecture and two training phases are easy to follow, and the qualitative figures illustrate all four tasks. Ablations cover the alignment objective, encoder freezing, LLM size, projector depth, and Stage-1 initialization.
weaknesses: The experimental comparisons are not consistently controlled. BrepCoder receives the complete target B-rep for completion and correction, whereas completion baselines receive a textual description and correction baselines receive one rendered image; ReCAD additionally uses a different dataset and language. These results establish the value of richer B-rep input, but do not cleanly isolate the proposed architecture or training strategy.

Evidence for the central claim that Stage-1 reverse-engineering pretraining enables downstream generalization is mixed. Removing Stage 1 changes completion by only 0.43 command-accuracy points and 0.03 parameter-accuracy points, while improving error-correction command accuracy and invalid ratio. The substantial CAD-QA gain is encouraging, but should be supported by repeated runs or uncertainty estimates.

The evaluation protocol lacks important details needed for reproducibility: optimizer and learning rates, epoch counts, batch sizes, decoding settings, corruption sampling, task mixture or whether Stage-2 tasks are trained separately, parameter-tolerance value, and compute requirements are not reported. No code/data-release statement is provided.

Several comparisons need statistical support. SGP-Bench contains only 1K models with a stated 10% test split, so the 79% versus 81% CAD-QA difference may correspond to only two questions. There are no confidence intervals, multiple seeds, or significance tests for any task.

The invalid-ratio reporting appears inconsistent: reverse-engineering baselines have values such as 12.08 and 13.98, while BrepCoder has 0.009, suggesting possible percentage-versus-fraction mixing. This must be clarified because the paper emphasizes the apparent orders-of-magnitude improvement. There is also a completion inconsistency between Table 2 (92.69) and Table 3 (92.96).

As an Algorithms/General contribution, the technical novelty is moderate: UV-Net encoding, CoCa alignment, an MLP projector, Qwen, and CAD-Llama's code representation are largely established components. The main novelty is their integration and multi-task application. Testing distribution shift, real industrial B-reps, more complex operations, unseen task transfer, or robustness to noisy B-reps would make the claimed general-purpose CAD-agent impact substantially more convincing.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant computer-vision/CAD problem: directly reasoning over industry-standard B-rep geometry rather than relying on rendered images or point clouds.

BrepCoder provides a coherent integration of a UV-Net B-rep encoder, CoCa-style code alignment, a projector, and a pretrained code-capable LLM. Encoding design histories as Python-like programs is well motivated.

Reverse-engineering results are strong: BrepCoder substantially improves median Chamfer distance over CADCL (0.464 vs. 0.972, scaled by 10^-3), reduces invalid outputs to 0.86%, and attains the best parameter accuracy and VLM score, although its command accuracy is slightly lower.

The evaluation covers reverse engineering, completion, error correction, and CAD-QA, with executable-code validity, geometric distance, sequence metrics, visual assessment, and useful qualitative examples of non-unique modeling histories.

Ablations examine alignment, encoder initialization and architecture, freezing, LLM backbone and scale, projector depth, and Stage-1 pretraining. The supplement provides important training hyperparameters and additional qualitative examples.
The method achieves competitive CAD-QA accuracy with a relatively compact 1.5B backbone, and the manuscript is generally clear and visually polished.
weaknesses: The central claim of a unified, general-purpose CAD agent is not convincingly demonstrated. The downstream tasks appear to use separate task-specific fine-tuning runs, with different epoch and batch-size settings; the paper does not evaluate one jointly trained checkpoint, task switching without retraining, or transfer to unseen tasks.

Completion and error correction provide the target model's complete B-rep alongside incomplete or corrupted code. This representation contains essentially the full answer geometry, making both tasks close to conditional reverse engineering. Comparisons against CAD-Llama using only a coarse text description and commercial MLLMs using a single rendered image therefore do not isolate architectural or reasoning gains and are not modality-matched.

Evidence for broad engineering reasoning and generalization is limited to DeepCAD's relatively simple synthetic sketch-and-extrude programs and a 1K-model multiple-choice QA benchmark. There is no evaluation on real industrial B-reps, out-of-distribution topology, more advanced CAD operations, noisy/imported geometry, or a separate dataset.

The claimed importance of Stage-1 structural-logic acquisition is only weakly supported for the code tasks: completion improves by just 0.43 ACCcmd and 0.03 ACCparam; error-correction ACCcmd becomes worse and ACCparam improves only 0.21. No multiple-seed results, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests are reported, so these small changes may be noise. The larger QA gain is promising but does not establish the claimed mechanism.

Several comparisons require stronger controls. ReCAD uses another dataset and is explicitly not directly comparable; GPT/Gemini receive less informative inputs; and the paper does not adequately detail the retraining, capacity, or hyperparameter parity of the modified DeepCAD and Brep2Seq baselines.

Evaluation reporting is incomplete. Median Chamfer distance can hide severe failures, command matching is ambiguous when sequence lengths or orders differ, and the GPT-5 visual score lacks the exact prompt, sampling configuration, repeated judgments, or human validation. Dataset split construction and possible near-duplicate leakage are also not analyzed.

Technical and reproducibility details remain unclear, including how the global 1x128 feature is concatenated with N node features, handling of variable face counts and context limits, the multimodal decoder's stated use of the EOS code embedding as a query during autoregressive captioning, task prompts, perturbation generation, inference settings, and code/model availability.

The technical novelty is moderate because most components—UV-Net, CoCa alignment, an MLP projector, Qwen, and the Python-like representation—are adopted from prior work. The main contribution is their integration and application breadth, so the overstated generalization claims and evaluation confounds materially weaken the case for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: directly reasoning over industry-standard B-rep geometry rather than relying only on images or point clouds. Covering reverse engineering, completion, error correction, and CAD question answering within a common B-rep/LLM framework is potentially useful.

The proposed pipeline is coherent, combining a UV-Net encoder, CoCa-style code alignment, a projector, and a pretrained code-capable LLM. The Python-like representation is interpretable and produces substantially fewer invalid programs than the sequence baselines.

Reverse-engineering results on DeepCAD are promising. BrepCoder reports the best parameter accuracy, median Chamfer distance, invalid ratio, and VLM score, while the discussion and examples appropriately recognize that command-level accuracy can penalize geometrically equivalent construction histories.

The paper includes several relevant ablations covering alignment, encoder initialization, encoder architecture, loss choice, encoder freezing, LLM backbone and size, projector depth, and Stage-1 pretraining. The supplementary material also provides training hyperparameters and additional qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The central claim of a unified multi-task model is not convincingly demonstrated. The manuscript says that Stage 2 fine-tunes the model for each downstream task and reports task-specific epoch and batch-size configurations, but never clearly establishes that one jointly trained checkpoint performs all tasks. If separate checkpoints are used, this is closer to a shared initialization than the claimed unified general-purpose CAD agent.

The downstream tasks are constructed so that the model receives the target final B-rep together with partial or corrupted code. Completion and synthetic error correction can therefore largely reduce to reconstructing code from the same B-rep learned in Stage 1. This does not establish correction of realistic modeling mistakes or completion from an intermediate design state whose intended final geometry is unavailable. The synthetic perturbations are also insufficiently specified and evaluated.

Evidence for the claimed benefit of the two-stage strategy is weak outside CAD-QA. Removing Stage 1 changes completion accuracy only marginally, and it actually improves command accuracy for error correction. No repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests are provided, so the small differences supporting several conclusions may be noise.

The evaluation is narrow relative to the industrial and generalization claims. Nearly all code-generation evidence comes from the synthetic and constrained DeepCAD distribution; there are no experiments on real-world CAD repositories, unseen operation families, noisy B-reps, distribution shifts, or substantially more complex construction histories. CAD-QA uses only about 100 test models under the stated split.

Some comparisons are not controlled. ReCAD uses another dataset and representation, while GPT and Gemini receive a single rendered image instead of the B-rep available to BrepCoder, making their large performance gap unsurprising. The retraining protocol and tuning budget for modified DeepCAD/Brep2Seq baselines are not sufficiently detailed. The proprietary GPT-5 visual score lacks the evaluation prompt, repeatability analysis, and validation against human judgments.

Important technical and reproducibility details are missing or ambiguous: the parameter tolerance delta is not reported; decoding settings and prompts are absent; the exact trainable LLM components are unclear; random seeds and variance are omitted; and no code or processed-data release is stated. The CoCa description is also internally unclear because the multimodal decoder is said to use only the EOS embedding as its query while Eq. 4 assumes autoregressive token-level conditioning. Overall, assessed as the default Algorithms/General type, the work has a useful integration and encouraging numbers, but the evidence does not yet substantiate its main unified, general-purpose, and industrial claims.

strengths: Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the paper presents a useful and reasonably original integration of B-rep encoding, CAD-code alignment, and a pretrained language model. Treating procedural CAD histories as Python-like code is well motivated and practically relevant.

The method is clearly structured: CoCa-style alignment first connects UV-Net B-rep features to CAD code, followed by reverse-engineering pretraining and downstream adaptation. The manuscript explains the principal architectural components and objectives sufficiently well.

The reverse-engineering results are strong. BrepCoder obtains the best reported parameter accuracy, median Chamfer distance, invalid ratio, and VLM score in Table 1, including a substantial median-CD improvement over CADCL (0.464 versus 0.972, both scaled by 10^-3). The 0.86% invalid ratio is particularly encouraging for executable CAD generation.

The evaluation covers several relevant capabilities—reverse engineering, completion, error correction, and CAD question answering—and includes both sequence-level and geometry-level metrics. The discussion and supplementary examples appropriately recognize that CAD construction sequences are non-unique, making geometric fidelity an important complement to exact command accuracy.

The ablations are informative and examine alignment pretraining, encoder initialization and architecture, CoCa versus CLIP, encoder freezing, LLM size and family, projector depth, and the effect of Stage-1 pretraining. The large degradation without Phase 1 provides good evidence that explicit B-rep/code alignment matters.
The use of a compact 1.5B backbone is appealing: it reaches 79% CAD-QA accuracy, close to the reported 81% of the substantially larger 7B PointLLM, while also supporting code-generation tasks.
weaknesses: The central claim of a unified multi-task model is not fully established. Section 4.1 states that completion, correction, and CAD-QA are trained for different numbers of epochs and that validation-selected weights are used for each task, which appears to imply separate task-specific fine-tuned checkpoints. The paper should explicitly state whether one set of weights performs all tasks and, if so, report joint multi-task results and interference; otherwise the contribution is better described as a shared architecture and initialization rather than a unified agent.

Completion and error correction are conditioned on the B-rep of the correct final object. This supplies essentially the complete target geometry, making both tasks close to reverse engineering with an auxiliary partial or corrupted program. In realistic incomplete or erroneous designs, the intended final B-rep may not be available. The paper should justify this setting, clarify the intended deployment scenario, and compare against a B-rep-only reverse-engineering model to quantify how much the partial or corrupted code actually contributes.

Several comparisons are not fully controlled. CAD-Llama receives a textual description rather than B-rep geometry; GPT-5 and Gemini receive a single rendered image; and ReCAD uses a different dataset that the authors themselves acknowledge prevents direct comparison. The retrained B-rep baselines are more relevant, but their fusion designs, parameter counts, training budgets, and tuning procedures are insufficiently specified to establish equal treatment.

The claimed benefit of Stage-1 pretraining is mixed for the code-generation tasks: in Table 3(b), completion improves only from 92.53 to 92.96 command accuracy and from 87.91 to 87.94 parameter accuracy, while error-correction command accuracy decreases from 99.43 to 99.08. The stronger changes in geometric metrics and CAD-QA are promising, but the paper overstates uniformly strong transfer and provides no multiple-seed variance or significance analysis.

The evidence is restricted mainly to DeepCAD, whose procedurally generated sketch-and-extrude models cover a limited portion of industrial B-rep complexity. There is no evaluation on real-world CAD, unfamiliar operation types, distribution shifts, or substantially more complex topology. Consequently, claims about broad industrial applicability and a general-purpose CAD agent remain preliminary.

CAD-QA uses only 1,000 models with an 80:10:10 split, leaving approximately 100 test examples. A two-percentage-point difference therefore has high uncertainty, yet no confidence intervals, multiple splits, or repeated runs are reported. The construction and balance of the questions and the exact retraining protocol for the point-cloud baselines also need more detail.

Some methodological and reproducibility details remain ambiguous: how the global shape feature is concatenated or broadcast across face embeddings; how variable-length sequences are aligned for command and parameter accuracy; the precise multimodal-decoder inputs, since the prose describes the EOS embedding as its query despite the autoregressive loss conditioning on preceding tokens; VLM evaluation prompts and repeatability; random seeds; and whether code, converted data, and trained checkpoints will be released. These issues are likely correctable but currently hinder verification.
